constructs
a distribution over finite control sequences by exponentially tilting a
reference distribution toward low-cost trajectories. A shifted Gaussian
proposal makes these trajectories easier to sample. Importance weights then
correct for the change of proposal, and their weighted perturbations update
the nominal sequence. The controller applies its first action and shifts the
remaining sequence to initialize the next optimization.

This calculation shares an exponential form with the policies derived from
entropy regularization, but the distributions and optimization problems
require separate definitions. SAC regularizes a state-conditional action
policy. The information-theoretic MPPI construction regularizes a distribution
over trajectories relative to a specified reference law

,
the reference law is generated by an uncontrolled
diffusion, and the quadratic control cost must match its noise covariance.
Neither derivation identifies an arbitrary MPPI implementation with SAC or
PCL’s soft Bellman solution.

The Gaussian mean update fits the tilted trajectory distribution by minimizing
KL divergence from that distribution to the Gaussian family. It need not
minimize the original expected-cost objective over Gaussian policies. Its
sampled implementation also has discretization and finite-sampling error.

An actor network distributes computation across training examples and returns
an action through a forward pass. MPPI spends model evaluations at the current
state, with a warm start from the previous plan. A new cost function can be
used in its next optimization, although finite computation and a poor proposal
can still prevent a useful update.

The methods developed in this chapter all parameterize policies, but they remain rooted in the Bellman equation. NFQCA, DDPG, TD3, and SAC learn Q-functions through successive approximation, then derive policies by maximizing these Q-functions. PCL minimizes a path residual derived from the soft Bellman equation. The policy serves as an amortized optimizer for a value-based objective.

What does this mean for reinforcement learning? The Euler approach shares the amortization idea: learn a policy network that directly outputs actions. But the training objective comes from first-order optimality conditions rather than from Bellman residuals or Q-function maximization. Whether Euler-style objectives give useful training signals for actor-critic methods, and whether first-order conditions help when the dynamics are known or learned, are open questions; the two traditions have had little contact.

SAC converts the soft value integral into an expectation under a learned
stochastic policy. PCL instead minimizes a multi-step consistency residual, and
MPPI updates a finite-horizon trajectory distribution at each decision. The Euler approach supplies a further alternative: solve a
first-order policy equation rather than a Bellman fixed point.

MPPI avoids a persistent actor approximation by performing online sampling
and optimization. Its exponential weights resemble those of entropy-regularized
policies, but its reference distribution, horizon, and sampling assumptions
define a different optimization problem. Finite computation and model error
remain in either approach.

All of these objectives retain an optimality equation derived from a value or
path-consistency relation. Can expected return be differentiated directly
without first treating a Bellman equation as the training objective?

Contrast MPPI and an actor network in terms of online computation and approximation error.

MPPI spends many model rollouts at every decision and avoids a persistent
actor approximation, but retains model, discretization, proposal, and
finite-sampling errors. An actor is cheap online but can introduce error
because its parameters only approximate the desired decision rule. A
warm-started MPPI sequence and a trained actor reuse computation in different
ways.
